activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: Laundry is sorted by colour because new dark or bright clothes can release dye into the wash water, and that dye can tint white and pale clothes.
story:
Everly sat on the bench at the bus stop with her gym bag open in her lap, turning her white school shirt over in her hands. It wasn't white anymore. The collar and one whole sleeve had come out of the wash a pale, cloudy pink, like a sunset that had given up halfway. She held it up to the light from the streetlamp and frowned.

"That looks like a failure," said Emelia, dropping onto the bench beside her with her own bag. "What happened to it?"

"I washed it. That's all. My mom's away this week, so I did my own laundry for the first time." Everly dug through the gym bag and pulled out a single red sock, still damp, and laid it on the shirt. The pink patches lined up almost exactly with where the sock had been tangled in the sleeve. "I found this stuck inside the shirt when I pulled everything out."

Emelia leaned over. "So the sock did it? It's brand new, isn't it?"

"Got it Saturday." Everly turned the sock in her fingers, then rubbed a damp corner of it against her wrist. A faint smudge of red came off onto her skin. "It's still letting dye go. The sock must have bled dye into the wash water, and the shirt soaked it up." She stared at the sock, working it through. New clothes, dark or bright ones, gave up dye. That dye sat in the water. Anything white or pale in that same water drank it in. Which meant the sorting her mother always did, the piles on the basement floor, wasn't just fussiness. It was a rule with a reason behind it.

"So that's why my mom separates everything," she said slowly. "I dumped it all in one load because it was faster. Darks, whites, everything." She folded the ruined shirt over her arm. "Next time I sort first. Colours with colours, whites on their own, at least until a new thing's been washed a few times."

"Could you fix the shirt?" Emelia asked.

Everly considered it. "I could wash it again on its own and see if the pink comes out. If it doesn't, it deteriorates into my painting shirt for art class." She smiled a little at that. "Ms. De Vries says we shouldn't ruin good clothes in the studio anyway. This way I'd have one that's already half-ruined and sort of an artisan tie-dye, and I wouldn't have to care."

The bus rounded the corner, its headlights sweeping across the wet road, and Everly zipped the sock into a side pocket by itself, away from everything else. "Travelling alone," she told it. "You're a menace."

Emelia laughed as they stood. "You're going to be so careful with laundry now."

"Careful and smug," Everly said, and slung her bag over her shoulder.

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: Two players can have the same average while one is steady and the other swings between great and terrible games, since an average hides how spread out the results are.
story:
Mya spread the stat sheets across the lunch table outside the gym, weighting the corners with her water bottle against the wind. The three-on-three tournament started Friday, and each team could add one player from the spare list. Two names kept circling in her head: Dani, who was not on the allowed list of named friends but whose numbers were right there, and a boy whose row Mya tapped with her pencil. "Both average ten points a game," she said to Isa. "Exactly the same. Ten and ten."

Isa leaned over the game-by-game column. "Look at this, though." She traced her finger down the page. The boy had scored two, then eighteen, then zero, then twenty. Up and down, up and down, like a heartbeat monitor. Dani's column read nine, ten, eleven, ten, nine. "Same average," Isa said slowly, "but one of them swings between great games and terrible ones."

Mya wrote both columns out again on a napkin, testing the idea. If she picked the steady one, her team could plan around a reliable ten points every game. If she picked the other, she might get twenty, or she might get nothing at all. The average hid all of that. It squished every game into a single number, the same way the news said the class average was 78 percent without saying who struggled and who breezed through. On the pollinate poster in the science hallway, the numbers about the bees hid the same kind of thing, she thought: the bees that visited a hundred flowers one day and slept the next. She crossed out the swingy column and circled the steady one.

Marc-Antoine dropped his tray next to hers, glanced at the napkin, and grinned. "You're overthinking it. I'll take the swingy one, and Mr. Das can put you down for steady." He signed the roster first, sliding it across the table toward the coach's office, which used to be the old residence of the caretaker before the school converted it. Mya signed beneath him and added Dani's name in careful block letters.

"It's not overthinking," she said, folding the napkin into her pocket. "It's the most fundamental decision of the whole tournament."

Saturday morning, in the first game, Marc-Antoine's pick threw up an air ball, missed two layups, and sat down with his hood up after four points. Mya's Dani scored nine, exactly as always, and their team won by one. Then Mya went out for the second game, took her first shot, and banked in a three she hadn't meant to bank, then missed everything else until the final buzzer. Marc-Antoine leaned over from the next court. "Ten points a game," he called out. "Same average as Dani."

activity: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition
knowledge_domain: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition
fact: Erosion is the wearing away and carrying off of rock and soil; deposition is the dropping of that material somewhere else.
story:
Isabella crouched over a narrow stream of seawater that ran across the sand toward the ocean, carrying tiny grains with it in a hurry. Her science notebook lay open beside her towel, and at the top of the page, in letters she had pressed so hard the pencil had nearly torn the paper, were the words: Explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years. Tomorrow. Out loud. In front of everyone.

"You look pessimistic," said Alessia, dropping down beside her with a slushie. "Like the slushie is going to spill on your notebook."

"The slushie might spill on my notebook," Isabella said. "But that is not my problem. My problem is that I have to explain something that takes millions of years, and I have one night, and every time I try to picture it my brain shows me a river holding a chisel."

Valentina waded over from the shallows, shaking water off her ankles. "Then don't picture a chisel. Watch your little river. It's doing the whole thing right now, just small." She knelt and dug her finger into the stream's path. The current slid around the blockage, then slowly, grain by grain, undercut the sides of her finger-dam until it collapsed and swept the sand downstream.

Isabella sat up straight. She grabbed a handful of wet sand and packed it into a wall a little farther along. "Okay. Test." The stream pushed against the wall, thinning it, pulling grains off the upstream face and carrying them away. Where the water slowed on the far side, the grains settled out and built a small sandy fan. "It took stuff from one place and dropped it in another."

"That's erosion," Alessia said, pointing at the worn wall. "Wearing away the rock and soil, and carrying it off."

"And deposition," Valentina said, pointing at the fan. "Dropping the material somewhere else."

Isabella wrote both words in her notebook, then drew arrows. "So a real river does this forever. Millions of years. Little scratches turn into a canyon this deep." She held her hands apart, then wider, then comically wider, until her arms were stretched like a bird about to take off, and Alessia laughed so hard she nearly spilled the slushie, which Isabella snatched off the sand just in time.

"There is an irony here," said Ms. Pritchard, the lifeguard, walking past with her thermos. "The girl worried about one night of homework just discovered something that takes a million years by playing in a puddle."

That evening, back at the beach to verify her idea one more time, Isabella found her notebook gone. She spun in a circle, heart pounding, until she spotted it fifteen meters down the beach, dry and undamaged, sitting on a low ridge of sand. The tide had come in, pulled sand from one stretch of beach, and dropped it right there, building the ridge around her book. She picked it up, hugged it, and ran up the slope, calling over her shoulder, "Alessia! The ocean just deposited my homework!"

activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
knowledge_domain: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
fact: Running the second half of a race faster than the first is called a negative split; running the first half faster is called a positive split.
story:
Dominic stood at the starting line of the school gym with his heart already running faster than his legs. Mr. Levy had taped four orange cones into a rough oval across the floor, and today was the last practice before Friday's eight-hundred-metre race against Riverside. Two laps around the cones, all-out, and Dominic had lost every time trial for three weeks by blowing up on the second lap.

"You went out like your shoes were flammable," Sahib said, clicking the stopwatch after the last attempt. "First lap forty-two seconds, second lap sixty-one. You died out there."

Ricky flopped onto the bleachers beside them, still breathing hard from his own trial. He held up his phone, where he'd typed both his laps. "Look at mine. First lap fifty-five, second lap fifty-three." He grinned through his sweat. "Running the second half faster than the first is called a negative split. Running the first half faster is called a positive split. Coach said that's why I passed you at the end."

Dominic stared at the two sets of numbers. In every race he'd ever lost, the pattern was the same: fast first lap, crawling second. He had always blamed his legs, or the stuffy air in the gym, or the squeak of his sneakers on the polished floor. But maybe the problem wasn't his legs at all. Maybe the hidden variable was how he spent the first lap, like pouring out the whole bottle before the race was half over. He needed a test.

"One more," he told Sahib. "Count my first lap out loud. If I'm under fifty, I'm going too hard, and I'll ease off until you say fifty-one."

Sahib raised an eyebrow but got the stopwatch ready. The gym smelled like floor wax and old rubber, and the afternoon light through the high windows made long stripes across the cones. Dominic crouched, started, and forced himself to hold back even when his body begged to sprint. "Forty-nine," Sahib called. Dominic shortened his stride. "Fifty-two at the lap." He had never run a first lap that slow on purpose, and it felt almost wrong, like tiptoeing when everyone else was running.

Then the second lap began, and his legs still had something left in them. He pushed through the final turn, arms pumping, lungs burning but working, and crossed the line without staggering. Sahib stared at the watch. "Fifty-one and fifty. You almost even split. And your total time? Two seconds faster than your best."

Ricky jogged over, phone in hand. "Dude. If you can persevere through one more week of going out slow, you might actually negative split on Friday."

Dominic looked down at the stopwatch, at those two small numbers side by side, the second one smaller than the first. His whole plan for the race had just flipped inside out. "Same pace tomorrow," he said, and picked up the cones.

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: One-point perspective works when you face straight down a street, so the fronts of objects face you and everything else recedes to one point.
story:
Adam had one goal in art class: draw the dragon street from his favorite game, the one where buildings lean in from both sides and every window glows like a hundred small furnaces. Ms. Bondarenko had written "one-point perspective" on the board and drawn a single dot in the middle of a rectangle, but Adam was already three pencils deep into his own version, and something was wrong.

The buildings on the left of his drawing looked fine. The ones on the right looked melted, like they had been left in the sun. Samantha leaned over from the next table, squinting. "It looks like the street got scared and ran away sideways."

"Maybe I just need to modify the windows," Adam said, and he redrew them, tilted the other way. Worse. Now the dragon street looked like it had two broken hips.

Ryerson strolled by with his coffee-stained thermos, because eighth graders apparently had a census of every bad drawing in the room and he was conducting it. "Nice attempt. Not plausible. Not even a little."

Adam ignored him, which was hard, because Ryerson was annoyingly often right. Adam sat back and stared at the dot on the board. All the guide lines in Ms. Bondarenko's example ran to that one point. Straight lines, like train tracks converging somewhere impossibly far away. Then he thought about the actual corner near his house, where he'd stood last weekend sketching. He had been standing at the corner, looking down one street with another street shooting off to his left. Two streets. Two directions. One dot. He counted on his fingers, which Samantha noticed and generously did not mention.

"That's it," he said. "You can't draw a corner with one vanishing point. One-point perspective works when you face straight down a street. The fronts of the buildings face you, like flat cards, and everything else, the roofs, the road, the sides, all of it recedes to that single point behind." He said it fast, like the words were escaping before he could lose them.

He flipped to a fresh page and imagined himself standing in the middle of the dragon street instead of at its corner. He drew the dot first, right in the center, then made the flat fronts of the buildings, then let every angled edge race toward the dot. The road narrowed to a spear point. The glowing windows shrank as they went. Far down at the dot he placed one tiny door, and behind it, he decided, the dragon.

Ms. Bondarenko paused at his table, tapped the page once, and said, "You discovered that the hard way, didn't you."

"Two broken hips," Adam said, "and a corner near my house."

Ryerson leaned in for a closer look at the little glowing door. "So what's behind it?"

Adam grinned and drew one golden eye peeking out at the vanishing point.

activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
knowledge_domain: going away to summer camp for the first time
fact: In parts of North America, blacklegged ticks, also called deer ticks, can spread Lyme disease, so campers there check their skin and hair for ticks after hiking through woods or tall grass.
story:
The camp bus smelled like sunscreen and granola bars, and William had spent the first hour memorizing the back of the seat in front of him. His mother had packed his duffel with the optimism of an entrepreneur who believes every product will sell, including three ponchos for a week of forecast sun. Across the aisle, Lennox was holding court about the camp brochure. "Nightly tick checks," he said. "The whole cabin lines up and somebody looks behind your ears. I'm skipping it. Ticks only get you if you're, like, wrestling a deer."

Lauralie, two rows up, turned around. "My cousin goes to this camp. She says the ticks there are blacklegged ticks. Some people call them deer ticks." She shrugged. "Different name, same tick. And in this part of North America they can give you Lyme disease, so everybody checks."

"Everybody but me," Lennox said. "I'll stay on the gravel."

William looked out the window at the fields rolling past, waist-high grass everywhere, and thought about it. If ticks lived in tall grass, then anybody walking through grass could pick one up, not just deer wrestlers. It was a rule you couldn't see working; you'd have to test it. When the bus stopped at a rest area with a picnic area framed by a sea of grass, he had his chance.

"I'm going to demonstrate something," he announced, and walked straight into the grass while Lennox watched from the safety of the pavement. William counted to sixty, came back, and sat on the curb. He pulled off one sneaker, then the sock, and turned the sock inside out in the transparent light of the afternoon sun. Near the toe, small as a sesame seed, something dark was crawling.

"Okay," Lennox said. His voice had gone up half an octave. "Okay, that's on your sock, that doesn't mean anything."

William flicked the tick onto the pavement and put his sock back on, methodically, like a scientist filing data. He didn't say anything, which was the whole trick. The bus driver called everyone back aboard, and as they filed on, Lennox studied the grass along the path with the expression of a man rethinking his entire worldview. He had walked through that same grass when he'd gone to look at the vending machines.

At the campground, when Ms. Sharma, the cabin leader, called for the nightly tick check, Lennox was second in line, ahead of William. "Check behind my ears twice," he said. "And my hairline. And everywhere else."

"First-timer?" Ms. Sharma asked, already parting his hair with two fingers.

"Let's just say I've revised my position," Lennox said, holding still, eyes closed, like a man praying.

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: A name a group uses for itself is called an endonym, and a name outsiders use for it is an exonym; Germans call their country Deutschland, while English speakers say Germany.
story:
Antoine raised his hand halfway, then lowered it. Mr. Cohen had asked the class to talk about where their families came from, and Antoine was still thinking about Sunday dinner, when his cousin visiting from Germany had laughed so hard she nearly knocked over her glass. The family kept calling her country Germany, and every time they did, she said "Deutschland" back, like she was correcting a nickname she hated. Antoine had not understood the joke, and it bothered him for three days.

"Antoine?" Mr. Cohen said. "You look like you're somewhere else."

"I'm here," Antoine said. "I just have a question. My cousin laughs when we say Germany, because she calls it Deutschland. Why do we have a word for a place that the people who live there don't use?"

Francesca turned around in her seat. "My mom does the same thing. She's from Côte d'Ivoire, and she gets annoyed when people say Ivory Coast."

"That's an exonym," Ross said suddenly, sitting up straighter. "A name outsiders use for a place or a group. The name a group uses for itself is an endonym. I read about it last week." He had been quiet all class, but now he was leaning forward over his notebook. "I was going to do my presentation on my grandpa's village, and I wanted the real name in it, not the English one. I looked it up."

Mr. Cohen nodded but said nothing more, which Antoine took as permission to keep going. Antoine flipped his notebook to a blank page and wrote two columns. At the top of one he wrote "their own name" and at the top of the other he wrote "our name." He tapped Ross's shoulder. "Test it. Go around the room."

Ross asked Francesca first, then the boy by the window, then Antoine himself, whose grandmother still called her island by its old name in her language while the atlas said something else. The columns filled up. Every single time, the two names were different. Antoine stared at the page and felt the pattern click into place, like a lock turning. It wasn't that his cousin was correcting them, exactly. She was just using the door she had always used, and his family was using the one built on the outside of the house.

"I thought she was being fussy," Antoine said slowly. "I'm going to stop saying Germany when she's here. I'll say Deutschland."

"It feels weird in your mouth at first," Francesca said. "But my mom lights up when someone tries." Ross grinned and drew a star next to the real name of his grandpa's village in his notebook, deciding on the spot that it would be the mandatory first slide of his presentation, the principle he'd build everything else around.

Antoine copied his two columns onto a clean sheet to show his cousin after school. At the bottom he wrote, in careful letters, "Deutschland," and underlined it twice.

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: Many school pools are 25 yards or 25 meters long, called short course, while Olympic swimming races are held in 50-meter pools, called long course.
story:
Andrew laced his skates on the cold bench outside Rink 2, where the hockey tryouts were supposed to start in twenty minutes, and tried not to look at the list pinned to the door. Forty-one names. Nineteen spots. His reputation at the rink was exactly one thing: the kid who fell through the bench door during last year's exhibition game and got waved at by the whole visiting team.

"Relax," said Mayson, who had come to watch even though she'd made the swim team on Monday. "You're fast when you stop thinking."

"That's the problem. I never stop thinking." He pointed his stick at her. "Speaking of which. That new girl, Rowan, said her old school time was two seconds faster than your tryout time, and now everyone says she's taking your spot in the medley relay."

Mayson's jaw tightened. "Her school had a fancy pool."

Andrew had never seen Rowan's school, but he chewed on the problem while the zamboni groaned past. Swimmers didn't slow down for no reason, and Rowan wasn't lying, he was pretty sure. So something invisible had to be different. He skated over to where Rowan was waiting for the figure skating session and asked her straight out how long her old pool was.

"Fifty meters," she said. "Our meets there were all long course."

"Ours is twenty-five yards," Mayson said, arriving with her bag. "Short course. Coach calls it that all the time."

Andrew held up his hands like he was measuring two different windows in the air. "So you're not comparing the same thing at all. Olympic swimming races are held in fifty-meter pools, long course, and our pool is half that, short course. It's like my old stick time from a rink with bigger ice. You can't just put the numbers next to each other."

Rowan looked almost relieved. "Nobody at my old school ever said that out loud."

They carried the idea to Ms. Shevchenko, who ran the pool schedule, and she nodded and posted both girls' times in separate columns with a note. By Tuesday the coaches were rethinking the relay. Mayson hugged Andrew so hard she knocked his helmet off, and Rowan got the backstroke leg after all, which meant Mayson gave up her favorite event to keep her.

At Thursday's hockey cut, Andrew survived the first round and then got spun into the boards during the last drill, and when the final list went up, his name was twenty-first. One spot short. He stood there while the zamboni came out again, and Mayson stood next to him, not saying anything helpful.

"Coach," Andrew called across the ice, "is the list final, or do you need a manager who knows how to measure things?"

The coach looked at him for a long moment, then tapped the clipboard. "Locker room, Monday. Bring a stopwatch."

activity: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
knowledge_domain: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
fact: Foreshadowing is a hint early in a story about something that will happen later, often noticed only on a second reading.
story:
Mr. Karimi handed out the story on Tuesday, four pages about a kingdom whose old dynasty was falling apart while an enemy army prepared to colonize the valleys to the south. He told the class to read it once for Tuesday and twice for Thursday. Alicia read it once Tuesday night, thought it was fine, and forgot about it until Thursday morning.

"Twice is pointless," she told Julianna in the hallway before class. "It's the same words both times."

"Then why'd he say it?" Julianna asked.

Alicia didn't answer, but in class, when Mr. Karimi asked them to write about how the author planted the ending early, she went back to page one just to prove nothing was there. In the first paragraph, the young prince kept a dead falcon on a shelf in his room, one whose wing had never healed right. She had skimmed past it Tuesday. She turned to the last page, where the prince's own broken messenger bird failed to fly, and the army arrived before any warning could be sent. She flipped between page one and page four three times.

"Jaycob," she whispered across the aisle. "The dead falcon at the start. Was that there the whole time?"

He leaned over. "The shelf bird? Yeah. I noticed it the second read. Foreshadowing."

"That's the word," Alicia said, and wrote it down. The falcon wasn't just a bird; it stood for the messenger system itself, winged and already failing, and the author had put it in the prince's bedroom before anything went wrong. She underlined the line about the unhealed wing and wrote "symbol of the whole kingdom" in the margin.

When Mr. Karimi called on her, she said the first-page falcon hinted at the ending, and that she had only caught it on the second reading because the first time she was rushing to find out what happened. He nodded once and wrote her example on the board.

After the bell, Julianna caught up with her at the lockers. "So the twice thing?"

"It's real," Alicia said. "The hint's sitting on page one and you walk right past it." She slung her backpack over one shoulder and pulled out the story again, turning back to the first page to see what else she had missed.

activity: to explain how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War
knowledge_domain: to explain how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War
fact: Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939, starting the Second World War in Europe, after Hitler demanded the return of Danzig and the Polish Corridor that Germany had lost at Versailles.
story:
Nathan had one afternoon to figure out his history presentation, and the school library had nothing but the internet, which kept giving him the same three sentences over and over. So he took the bus downtown to the city archive, where his friend Fares had once found his grandfather's name in a list of refugees from 1948. Fares had said the place smelled like dust and patience, and he was right. Behind the front desk, Mr. Santos was misting a tropical fern that leaned toward the window as if it missed somewhere warmer, and he raised an eyebrow when Nathan asked for "anything about Versailles, I guess."

"You guess," Mr. Santos repeated, but he was smiling, and he led Nathan to a long table and set down a folder of reproductions. "The maps are the good part. Start there." Nathan spread out a copy of a 1919 map of Europe and frowned at it. Germany looked like a vase that had been chipped on purpose. A thin strip of land ran from East Prussia down to the sea, cutting German territory in two, and two words were printed along it. Danzig. Polish Corridor.

Emy arrived twenty minutes later, out of breath, because she was his partner on the presentation and had sprinted from her piano lesson. "You started without me," she said, dropping her bag, then she saw the map and went quiet the way she did in museums. She put one finger on the corridor. "This is what he wanted back," she murmured, mostly to herself. Nathan leaned in. "Who wanted what back?"

She flipped open her notes, photocopies of newspaper pages from 1939. "Hitler demanded the return of Danzig and the Polish Corridor, the land Germany lost at Versailles." She traced the strip with her finger, up to the city on the coast and back down again. "And when Poland said no, Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939. That started the Second World War in Europe." Mr. Santos, passing by with his watering can, paused long enough to nod once, then kept walking.

Nathan sat back. He had been writing his presentation as a list of complaints, reparations, army limits, lost land, and it had felt like a pile of unrelated facts. Now the map showed him something he couldn't see on the screen at home: a strip on paper from 1919 turning into tanks twenty years later. He pulled out his notebook and drew the border himself, badly, then labeled it. "That's my first slide," he said. "The map first, then the demand, then the invasion." He underlined the date twice to emphasize it, hard enough that Emy winced.

"Don't kill the notebook," she said, and slid the 1939 clipping across the table so the two pages sat side by side, the border and the war touching at the edges. Mr. Santos came back with a second folder and set it down gently between them. "Keep going," he said. "You've got the shape of it."

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: A 2018 study by Jeffrey Hall of the University of Kansas found it takes about 50 hours together to turn an acquaintance into a casual friend.
story:
The new house smelled like paint and nothing else. Tristan walked through the empty living room, his sneakers echoing off the bare walls, and found a folded piece of paper taped inside the kitchen cabinet. Somebody had left it behind on purpose, he decided, because the tape was fresh and the fold was neat.

He opened it. "Dear whoever," the note read. "I'm Wassim. I lived here for six years and now I live in Arizona. I'm leaving you my bike lock combo (it's 22-10-7) and one piece of advice. There was a study in 2018 by Jeffrey Hall at the University of Kansas. He found it takes about 50 hours together to turn an acquaintance into a casual friend. I timed it with my best friend and he was right, almost to the hour. Good luck. P.S. There's a kid named Jasmin two houses down who is worth every minute."

Tristan read the note twice. Fifty hours. He had been dreading this move for weeks, ever since his dad announced the new job, because leaving his friends felt like a door slamming shut. Now he scrutinized the note like it was a math problem. One lunch period at his old school was thirty minutes. If fifty hours made a casual friend, then one lunch made exactly nothing, and his old friends should have been strangers forever. Except they weren't. Which meant the hours had been adding up all along, in class and at practice and on the bus, without anyone counting.

He found a pencil in a moving box and did the arithmetic on the back of the note. An afternoon with Jasmin might be three hours. Three hours was feasible this weekend. Three hours divided into fifty meant nearly seventeen afternoons, which felt impossible until he remembered that seventeen afternoons was really just a couple of months of Saturdays. He had been thinking of loneliness as a locked door, when it was more like a slow clock.

At first he didn't want to go knock on a stranger's door. That plan sounded like something from a movie, and movies were not real life. But all afternoon the note sat on the counter, and all afternoon the empty rooms echoed, and by dinner he had changed his mind. Unopened boxes could wait. A clock that hadn't started yet was worse than one ticking slowly.

Jasmin answered the door holding a half-assembled model rocket. "You're the new kid," she said. "From the empty house."

"Wassim's house," Tristan said. "He left me a note. And a math problem. How do you feel about Saturdays?"

Jasmin looked at him for a long second, then held up the rocket. "Saturdays work. You can hold the glue."

Behind her, on the porch railing, somebody had painted a small line of tally marks, dozens of them, with the number 50 circled at the end.

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: In email, BCC stands for 'blind carbon copy': people added in the BCC field receive the message, but other recipients cannot see their addresses.
story:
Anna sat at the kitchen table with her mother's laptop open to a blank email, the cursor blinking in the To field like it was waiting for her to decide something. Her birthday party was Saturday, and she wanted to invite the whole class, all twenty-six of them, but last month she had watched Noa get teased because a group email went out with everyone's addresses pasted in the To line, and one boy kept messaging people afterward pretending to be someone else. Anna had typed the whole list into the To field already, and now she stared at it, thinking about Noa's face at lunch that day, quiet, picking at her tray, saying only, "It's fine."

She highlighted the list and cut it, then pasted it into a strange little field labeled BCC instead. She had noticed the field weeks ago while helping her dad email the neighbors about the storm cleanup, and he had said only, "Put them there," without saying why. Now she wondered if it even did anything.

She typed a subject line first: "Anna's party, Saturday, 2 PM." For the message itself she tried three openings. "Come to my party!!!" felt too bouncy, like she was shouting, so she deleted it and wrote, "Hey everyone, I'm having a party Saturday. Hope you can come." That felt neutral, like her tone was sitting up straight instead of leaning on anyone. Under her breath she read it aloud, and it sounded like something a person would actually say.

Before sending, she needed to know if BCC actually worked, so she tested it. She sent the message to her own address with Adalyn's address in the BCC field, then signed out and checked Adalyn's account on her phone, since Adalyn had given her the password last spring to help with a science project. When the email arrived, she scrolled through the whole header. In the To line, on Adalyn's copy, only Anna's own address appeared. Adalyn's address was nowhere.

"So BCC hides them," Anna said to the empty kitchen. She remembered Adalyn at the school meeting in fall, standing up to advocate for a later lunch period for eighth graders, saying everyone deserved a private way to complain without being seen doing it. Maybe this was like that. Maybe Noa would rather come to the party without everyone knowing she was invited along with everybody else.

Anna deleted her test, pasted the class list into BCC, left the To field with only her own address, and clicked Send. Then she pushed the laptop aside carefully, the way her dad always reminded her, since the warranty on it only covered spills for another two months. Her phone buzzed almost at once. It was Noa: "got your email. only saw your address on it. smart." Anna smiled and typed back, "Saturday. 2 PM. Bring nothing but yourself."

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
knowledge_domain: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
fact: A 2001 study of school playgrounds found that when a classmate stepped in to stop bullying, the bullying stopped in more than half of the cases.
story:
Tyler had read the fact on a poster in the library and copied it into his notebook because the numbers surprised him: a 2001 study of school playgrounds found that when a classmate stepped in to stop bullying, the bullying stopped in more than half of the cases. More than half. That meant it didn't always work, but it worked most of the time, and he'd been turning that over in his head ever since, wondering if he'd ever have the nerve to test it.

The chance came at Finnley's birthday party, which was a slime-making party in the garage, eight kids around a folding table covered with newspaper. Tyler was squeezing glue into a cup when the boy next to him noticed Winnie's batch. Her slime had come out lumpy and gray instead of glossy, and the boy held his up beside hers. "Looks like something the dog threw up," he said, and a couple of kids laughed. Winnie stared at her cup and started folding her newspaper over it, hiding it, which was worse than the laugh.

Tyler's first idea was to resign himself to staying quiet, because the safe move was to laugh along or say nothing. But the poster floated back to him, more than half the time it works, and he thought about what "stepping in" might actually mean. Not a speech. Not yelling. Maybe just changing what the table was looking at. He held up his own cup, where he'd deliberately mixed in too much glitter. "Check out this disaster," he said. "I think I ruined the polymer. It's supposed to chain together, and mine just quit." Finnley leaned over to look, and then Winnie, still holding her folded newspaper, said quietly, "You added the saline too fast. That breaks the chains."

"Can you fix it?" Tyler asked her. She unfolded her paper, took his cup, and dribbled in the activator a drop at a time while the whole table watched. His slime pulled itself together into something robust and stretchy, and the gray lump of hers suddenly looked less important, because the girl who made the mistake was now the expert. The boy who'd made the dog joke didn't say anything else about it.

A few minutes later, that same boy knocked over his own cup with his elbow, and green slime slid across the newspaper toward Tyler's shoe. He froze, ears going red, waiting for someone to make it a joke. Winnie pushed the paper towel roll down the table to him without a word, and Tyler grabbed a wad and started blotting beside him. "Thanks," the boy muttered, and then, staring at his cup, "Winnie, could you maybe show me how you did the drops?"

She smiled and reached for his activator.

activity: to explain how nicotine causes addiction in the brain's reward pathway
knowledge_domain: to explain how nicotine causes addiction in the brain's reward pathway
fact: Dopamine release teaches the brain that a behavior is worth repeating, which is how nicotine use becomes a learned habit.
story:
Emmett sat in the dentist's waiting room with his health project folded into his back pocket, and every time he tried to say it out loud in his head, it came out like soup. Ms. Van Dijk had drawn one line on the board before the bell: Tomorrow, explain how nicotine hooks the brain. Then she had said, "If your listener still doesn't get it, you haven't explained it," and wiped the line away.

Kacey slid into the chair beside him, shaking rain off her jacket. "You look like you're going to be the one getting a tooth pulled."

"I have to explain nicotine addiction tomorrow and I don't actually understand it. It's all invisible. Brain, chemicals, whatever." He held up his phone. "Here's my only idea. Watch." He scrolled and stopped at random on a photo from last summer, then held the screen where she could see it. "Why do I keep checking this thing even when nothing new is there?"

"Because you're hopeless," Kacey said, but she took the phone and turned it over in her hands, thinking. She counted something under her breath. "Your median is like forty likes. That's the middle. Half your posts get more, half get less."

"So the ones that get more, I check them over and over. And the ones nobody liked, I forget them." Emmett leaned forward. "It's like the likes teach me which posts are worth repeating."

Behind the desk, the dental assistant called a name that wasn't his. Emmett's mom gave him a small nod, meaning she'd heard none of it and all of it at once.

"But where's the connection?" Kacey said. "Nobody likes a cigarette."

Emmett rubbed his jaw, where a dull ache had been building all week. "The likes aren't the thing itself. They're the message. When I see them, something in my head fires, and it transmits the signal that says, do that again. That's what I keep tripping on. Nicotine doesn't have to feel amazing. It just has to tap that same wire."

"So the brain learns it," Kacey said slowly, testing each word. "The dopamine," and she said the word carefully, "tells the brain the behavior is worth repeating. That's how it turns into a habit instead of a choice."

"That's it. That's the whole thing." Emmett grabbed a pen from his mom's bag and wrote it on his hand because the project was still in his back pocket and his hands were shaking a little. Kacey steadied the pen for him so the words wouldn't smear.

When the assistant finally called his name, Ms. Van Dijk was standing at the desk in her coat, her own six-month cleaning done. She raised an eyebrow at his inked hand as she passed. "Tomorrow, then."

"Tomorrow," Emmett said, and followed the assistant down the bright hallway, still mouthing the words.

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: At the Scripps National Spelling Bee, spellers may ask for a word's definition, part of speech, language of origin, or a sentence using it.
story:
Gavin stood at the microphone in the community center gym, and the word he got was "bazaar." His mind went blank. Two a's or three? He had studied every night for two weeks, and now the letters would not come.

Behind him, Adam sat with the other spellers, tapping his shoe against the folding chair. Jazmine had already survived her round. On the far wall, the clock ticked toward noon, and Mr. Li, who ran the center's study room, watched from the back with his arms folded.

Then Gavin remembered something Adam had told him on the bus. At the Scripps National Spelling Bee, spellers may ask for a word's definition, part of speech, language of origin, or a sentence using it. He had never tried it himself. Did the community center follow the same rules? He decided to find out.

"Can I have the language of origin?" he asked.

The judge blinked, then checked her sheet. "Persian." Gavin felt his grip loosen on the microphone. Persian words in English almost always came through the b-a-z-a-r spelling, like "caravan." He had seen that pattern in his word lists.

"Can I have a definition too?"

"A marketplace, especially in the Middle East."

"One more. A sentence?"

"The pilot bought a propeller-shaped keychain at the bazaar." A few parents laughed. Gavin pictured the word, then took a breath.

"Bazaar. B-A-Z-A-A-R. Bazaar."

"Correct," the judge said.

Adam exhaled loudly enough for the whole front row to hear, and Jazmine pumped her fist once, then tried to look neutral, like she had never doubted him. Mr. Li nodded from the back.

The next speller stepped up and got "voracious." He started too fast, without asking anything, and missed the second o. When Gavin's turn came around again, the judge gave him "nadir."

"The lowest point," Gavin thought, which was exactly where he refused to finish. He raised his hand before the clock could spook him. "Language of origin, please."

"Arabic."

Arabic, like bazaar. Single vowels, mostly. He asked for a sentence to buy himself a second. "The tired hikers would consume their last granola bar at the nadir of the trail." That was enough. He saw the word whole, the way he saw it on his flashcards.

"Nadir. N-A-D-I-R. Nadir."

"Correct."

Adam whispered, "That's my whole strategy you stole," and Gavin grinned and walked back to his chair, already listening for Jazmine's word.

activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
knowledge_domain: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
fact: Subtracting an element's atomic number from an atom's mass number gives the number of neutrons, because the mass number counts protons plus neutrons.
story:
Claire stared at the practice sheet Ms. Goh had handed out and felt like the periodic table was written in a language designed specifically to embarrass her. The little box for carbon showed a big 12 at the top and a smaller 6 above the symbol C, and she was supposed to find protons and neutrons, which nobody could see, from numbers that weren't labeled. Kyleigh, beside her, was already filling in answers like the sheet was a menu.

"The atomic number is the small one," Zia offered from across the lab table. "Six, for carbon. That's the protons."

"So the big twelve is..." Claire tapped her pencil on the 12. "Neutrons?" She wrote it down, then stopped. Zia made a face like someone watching a friend step on a rake.

Ms. Goh drifted by, but she only said, "Mass number," and kept walking, which was the most annoying possible amount of help. Claire glared at the box. Mass number. Twelve. Protons, six. If the mass number wasn't neutrons, and it wasn't protons, then it was probably both of them smooshed together, the way a porous sponge holds water in all its holes at once instead of in one tidy pocket. She tried it. Six protons plus six neutrons equals twelve, so twelve minus six gives the neutrons. She erased her answer and wrote six.

"Wait, say that again," Kyleigh said, leaning over. "You just subtract the atomic number from the mass number?" Claire showed her with the next element, oxygen, mass sixteen, atomic eight. Eight protons, and sixteen minus eight made eight neutrons. Kyleigh tried sodium on her own sheet and got eleven and twelve, then held it up like a trophy. "I have never enjoyed subtraction more in my life," she announced, loud enough that the boy at the next table looked over.

They raced through the rest of the rows. Zia, who was fast but competitive in a way that occasionally required Kyleigh to mediate disputes about who had called fluorine first, beat them by two elements. Claire didn't mind. She had been the one stuck twenty minutes ago, and now the hidden numbers were just sitting there waiting to be subtracted out, every single time.

At the end of class Ms. Goh collected the sheets, paused at Claire's, and raised an eyebrow. "All correct. Even uranium."

"Uranium was the easiest one," Claire said. "It's basically a carnivore. It just eats other numbers and leaves the neutrons behind."

Ms. Goh laughed, a short surprised bark, and Claire slid her worksheet to the top of the pile.

activity: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
knowledge_domain: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
fact: In American English, a comma or period that ends a quotation goes inside the closing quotation marks; British usage often places it outside.
story:
Noemie spread two copies of her story across the library table: the original she had sent to Yassin, and the version he had mailed back with every line of dialogue circled in red. He had moved to Manchester in October, and they had agreed to swap stories once a month. His note was clipped to the last page. "Your commas are all in the wrong place," it said. "Fix them."

She stared at her opening line. "Hand me the flashlight," she whispered. That was how she had written it, period inside the quotation marks. Yassin had crossed it out and moved the period to the other side, like this: "Hand me the flashlight". He had done the same thing with every comma. Twenty-one marks, all relocated.

Blakely dropped into the chair across from her and stole a rice cake from her lunch bag. "He thinks you can't punctuate?"

"He thinks I punctuate wrong on purpose, maybe." Noemie tapped the page. "Look. Every single one. That's not sloppiness. That's a pattern." She had learned in science that when something happens the same way every time, there's a rule behind it, even if you can't see the rule itself. So she tested it. She pulled the library's copy of a Harry Potter book off the shelf, found a line of dialogue, and checked. The British edition put the period outside the quotation marks. Then she pulled a novel by an American author and checked that too. Period inside.

"Two countries, two rules," she said.

"Prove it," Blakely said, mouth full.

Noemie raised her hand and walked to the desk, where Mr. Adebayo was stamping returns. "Is a comma that ends a quotation supposed to go inside the closing quotation marks?"

"In American English, yes," he said. "British usage usually puts it outside." He went back to stamping.

She returned to the table almost running. In her draft, her narrator's story was about two kids hiding during a recession, sneaking into an abandoned factory where the weather turned volatile and a storm tore the roof open. The climax scene was fine. The dialogue was not, at least not for a British reader. She took out a pen and, on a fresh sheet, wrote every line of dialogue twice, once each way.

"Which one are you sending back?" Blakely asked.

Noemie folded both versions together and slid them into an envelope. On the back she wrote, "You're right in Manchester. I'm right here. Pick a page."

Blakely laughed so loudly that Mr. Adebayo looked up, and Noemie pressed the envelope flat under her palm.

activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: Glasses for astigmatism use cylindrical lenses, which bend light more in one direction than in the other.
story:
Colton sat on the paper-covered bench in the nurse's office, a purple folder in his lap and a pair of new glasses in his hands. He had not wanted to come. For weeks the whiteboard had been a grey smear, and he had copied Cedar's notes without admitting why, until Mr. Van Dijk caught him squinting at a quiz and sent him down the hall with a note that read, in his careful handwriting, "Vision screening, please. C. has been guessing at distances."

The nurse, a small woman with reading glasses on a chain, had already done the screening. "Astigmatism," she said, sliding the new pair across the desk to him. "These are for you." The frames were plain and dark, and when he put them on, the whole room snapped into focus so sharply that he blinked. The poster of the food groups on the wall had actual words on it. The median strip of the hallway, visible through the open door, turned out to be painted yellow, not the muddy line he had always assumed it was.

Then he tilted his head, and the doorframe bent. The whole doorway stretched sideways like taffy. He straightened up, and it went back to normal. He tilted again, slower this time, and the stretching came back at the same angle. That was strange, because ordinary magnifying glasses made things bigger all over, not in just one direction. He turned the glasses ninety degrees on his face, holding the temples like a steering wheel, and the stretch flipped. Now the doorframe was tall and skinny instead of wide and melted. Whatever the lenses were doing, they were doing it along one line only.

He tried it with the clock. Straight on, the clock was a circle. Turned sideways, it became an egg. He took the glasses off, held one lens up to the window, and rotated it slowly, watching the flagpole outside lean and swell, lean and swell, like the lens had a grain in it, the way wood does. "Cylindrical," the nurse said when he asked, marking something in his folder. "Not perfectly round. They bend light more in one direction than in the other." Colton nodded and turned the lens again, watching the flagpole lean.

Kenza appeared in the doorway, jacket half on, holding out a folded paper. "Cedar sent this. You left before lunch." The note said, "Board duty is yours today. Copy everything, and this time read it yourself. Also, do you look like a professor now? Serious question."

Colton put the glasses back on, straight and careful, and looked down the hall at the yellow median line running clean and bright toward the gym. "Tell him yes," he said. "A completely authentic professor." He pulled the door closed behind him and walked the line all the way to the end.

activity: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why
knowledge_domain: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why
fact: Over the past century, U.S. stocks have earned higher average yearly returns than U.S. government bonds, but with much bigger drops along the way; the extra return rewards the extra risk.
story:
James spread the printouts across the food court table and tried to ignore the smell of cinnamon buns. His economics class had been split into two teams for a month-long investing game, and in twenty minutes Mr. Huang would meet them here to hear each side's final argument. James was on the stock team with Mason, and Lilith was on the bond team, and the scoreboard had flip-flopped so many times that nobody could call a winner yet.

"That's my dilemma," Mason said, jabbing a finger at the running total. "Some weeks we're way ahead, some weeks we're way behind. How do I argue we're better?"

James studied the zigzag line on the graph. Their team's returns rose higher than Lilith's team, over and over, but the drops were brutal, deep valleys that swallowed whole months of gains. Lilith's line was nearly flat, inching up a little at a time. He tapped the two lines. "Look, ours climbs higher on average. Hers barely dips."

"So we win," Mason said.

"So we fall harder," James said. "Both things are true at once."

Lilith slid into the seat across from them with her own folder. "I couldn't help overhearing. You sound pessimistic about your own team."

"I'm not pessimistic. I'm trying to figure out what risk actually means." James turned the graph toward her. "Your returns are lower than ours, year after year, but your drops are tiny. Ours are huge. That's the whole difference, isn't it? The extra return is like a reward for taking the extra risk." He paused, testing the idea against the numbers. "Over the past century, that's how it's gone. Stocks earned higher average yearly returns than government bonds, but with much bigger drops along the way."

"That's exactly what my notes say," Lilith said, surprised. "I was going to argue that bonds are safer."

"Then here's the problem," James said. "Mr. Huang's question is which one is riskier, and why. If we only say stocks are riskier, we lose. If we only say stocks earn more, we're hiding half the truth."

Mason had gone quiet, which was unusual. "So change the argument," he said finally. "Don't pick a side. Say the two things balance." He pulled a stack of napkins from the dispenser and began to distribute them, one sheet for each point they wanted to make, scribbling a headline on every napkin. James wrote beside him, and Lilith, instead of guarding her own team's secrets, added a number from her folder to one of their points.

"You're helping the competition," Mason said.

"You're getting it right," Lilith said. "That matters more."

When Mr. Huang arrived, carrying a tray and looking hurried, James stood up with the napkins in his hand, edges curled, ink already smudging. "We're ready," he said, and laid the first napkin on the table.

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: The U.S. agency NIOSH recommends limiting exposure to 85 decibels to eight hours a day, and each 3-decibel increase halves the safe listening time.
story:
Theodore tried on the third shirt of the evening and studied himself in the mirror. The first one had been too stiff, the second too bright, and this one, a plain blue button-down, seemed safe enough for a first school dance. He had spent a week anticipating this night, and now that it was actually here, he mostly wanted to stop thinking about it. From downstairs his mother called that she had picked up his antibiotic for the ear infection, the one the doctor had diagnosed on Tuesday, and that he was to take it with food even if he was out late. "It's ear medicine," he muttered to the mirror. "Figures."

The gym was louder than any room he had ever stood in. Braylon grabbed his sleeve and pulled him toward the far wall, where two giant speakers stood stacked like refrigerators, and Adelie followed with her phone out, filming the crowd. Within ten minutes Theodore's ears had begun to feel strange, a fuzzy fullness, like swimming underwater, and the edges of sound had gone soft. Braylon shouted something at him twice. The second time Theodore caught it: "Your ears do that too?"

They retreated to the water fountain, and it was there, holding cold paper cups, that Braylon said his father had a poster at the shop about noise. "It says NIOSH, that's a U.S. agency, recommends limiting exposure to 85 decibels to eight hours a day," he recited, the way he recited everything from his father's posters. "And every 3-decibel increase halves the safe listening time." Adelie frowned at him over her cup. "Halves it? So louder isn't just a little worse."

Theodore worked it through while the bass thumped through the floor. If those speakers were pushing well past 85 decibels, then the safe time wasn't hours anymore, it kept getting cut in half and cut again, until it might only be minutes standing right beside them. "That's why my ears felt weird right away," he said. "We weren't standing there for eight hours. We were standing there for two songs." He tested the idea by walking Adelie back toward the dance floor but steering wide of the speakers, keeping the whole crowd between them and the stacked cabinets. At that distance the music was still huge, but the fuzziness in his ears did not creep back, even after four more songs.

When his father picked him up at ten, Theodore slid into the passenger seat and found a transparent water bottle waiting for him in the cup holder, along with the antibiotic and a granola bar, because his mother never trusted a dance to include real food. "How was it?" his father asked, pulling away from the curb. Theodore thought of the speaker wall, of Braylon reciting his poster, of the exact spot on the floor where the music stayed big but his ears stayed quiet. "Good," he said. "We found the right place to stand."

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: In traditional Chinese culture white is worn for mourning at funerals, while in many Western weddings the bride wears white.
story:
Dinner was noodles with pork, and Annabelle slid the card across the table before anyone could pick up a fork. "It came today," she said. "From Auntie Mei."

Her mother read it aloud while Dad refilled the water glasses. "Dear everyone. Cousin Lin's wedding is in June. I know you will want to look your best, but please do not all arrive in white. In our family, white is worn for mourning at funerals. Lin has asked for red instead. Love, Auntie Mei."

"She means it," Grandma said, setting down her fork. "I wore white to bury my mother. Every stitch of it."

Annabelle looked at the card, then at Grandma, then at the picture on the fridge of her teacher Mr. Fraser's wedding, which her mother had pinned up because the cake had been magnificent. The bride in the photo wore white. Everybody at that wedding had said she looked like something out of a dream. Same color, two completely different ideas, and neither of them wrong, exactly. She turned her glass until it stood perpendicular to the placemat, just to have something to do with her hands while she thought.

"I'm going to presume," she said slowly, "that Lin's family will see white and think funeral, even if we mean wedding."

"Precisely," said Grandma.

"So we test it." Annabelle grabbed the notepad by the phone. "Everybody write down what white means to you. One word. Don't talk first, just write." Dad wrote something and folded his paper like it was a bet. Grandma wrote hers in characters Annabelle couldn't read, which she decided was fair. When they unfolded the papers, Dad's said "bride," Mom's said "clean," and her little brother, who was a committed carnivore and hadn't touched his noodles all night, had written "mayonnaise."

"Mayonnaise," Annabelle read out loud, and the table cracked up, even Grandma.

Then her phone buzzed on the tablecloth. A message from Elliot, whose family was from Glasgow: "What are you wearing to the wedding? My mum bought a white suit and she looks SO fancy." Annabelle typed back a photo of Auntie Mei's card. Three dots appeared, vanished, appeared again. "She says thank you and also oh no."

Annabelle smiled, but it faded a little. Auntie Mei would be relieved, and Elliot's mum would return a suit she'd loved, and Grandma would sit at the wedding in June without thinking even once of her own mother's grave, which was the whole point. You couldn't have all of it at once.

She looked around the table, everyone still laughing about mayonnaise, and held up her glass of water. "To Lin," she said. "Red for everybody."

"To Lin," they said, and clinked, glasses crossing above the noodles like little white bells.

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: In both 1995 and 1996 David Justice had a higher batting average than Derek Jeter, yet Jeter's average for the two years combined was higher.
story:
Justin had the laptop balanced on the arm of the couch, a notebook on his knee, and the living room TV paused on a baseball highlight. Oskar flopped into the recliner beside him, shaking a bag of chips.

"You said you found something weird," Oskar said, mouth full.

"Look at this." Justin turned the screen. "I'm comparing players for my fantasy draft. David Justice had a higher batting average than Derek Jeter in 1995. And Justice beat him again in 1996. Higher average both years."

"So Justice is better. Draft Justice's ghost, done."

"That's the thing." Justin scrolled, frowning. "When I add the two seasons together, Jeter's combined average is higher. Jeter wins overall."

Oskar leaned over and squinted at the numbers, then sat back. "That can't be right. You typed something wrong."

"That's what I thought." Justin reloaded the page, then checked a second site on his phone, then a third. Every source agreed: in both 1995 and 1996 David Justice had a higher batting average than Derek Jeter, yet Jeter's average for the two years combined was higher. "It's not a typo. It happens."

"How? Does the computer hibernate for a second and wake up dumb?" Oskar grabbed a chip. "Numbers don't flip like that."

"Numbers don't," Justin said slowly, "but averages aren't really numbers, are they? They're more like... one number wearing two seasons like a coat." He tapped his pen against the notebook. He tried a little test with made-up players, giving one lots of at-bats in a bad year and few at-bats in a great year. The combined average tipped the same strange way. So it wasn't about being better. It was about how the seasons got squeezed together, and how the squeezing wasn't fair.

The door opened and Deklan came in, dropping his backpack by the couch. "Ms. Levy kept us after class arguing about whether class rankings mean anything. She says one grade point average can hide a hundred different report cards. Chronic complainer, that woman."

"Wait, say that again," Justin said.

"One number hiding a hundred report cards. She says it like it's a crime."

Justin looked from Deklan to the screen. Averages did this everywhere, then. Not just baseball. He pulled up a news app and found a story ranking cities by safety, then another ranking schools by test scores, each one boiling a whole year of events down to a single line.

"Can you imagine if they had to show everything?" Deklan said, peering at the screen. "The whole messy pile?"

"Nobody would read it," Oskar said. "Nobody has that kind of leisure."

"Maybe," Justin said. He copied the Justice and Jeter numbers into his notebook, one season per column, and underlined the combined average twice. On Monday he was going to walk into Ms. Levy's class, put this on the board, and ask her how many other rankings were hiding a trick like this. "Draft Jeter," he told Oskar, and clicked the button.

activity: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs
knowledge_domain: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs
fact: In Spanish, "para llevar" means "to take away," so a customer who wants food to go asks for it "para llevar."
story:
Riley smoothed the paper menu on the cafeteria table and read it again for the third time. Mr. Robinson had turned the lunch period into a pretend restaurant for Spanish class, with students as waiters and cashiers, and everyone had to order entirely in Spanish. She had practiced her lines on the bus that morning, but now the words felt slippery, like they might slide right out of her head. "Quiero un sándwich de pollo," she whispered, testing it. Across the table, Caleb was drumming his fingers and glancing at the clock, because he wanted to finish eating fast enough to catch the last ten minutes of the basketball game on the gym TV.

Riley walked to the counter, where Kurtis stood in a paper hat, holding a pencil like a tiny sword. "Quiero un sándwich de pollo, por favor," she said. Kurtis nodded and scribbled on his notepad. Then came the part she had practiced hardest. "¿Cuánto cuesta?" How much does it cost? Kurtis answered, "Cuatro dólares," and Riley counted out the play money, adjusting the little pile of bills until it came to exactly four. She felt a small glow of triumph. One whole transaction, done.

Then the problem appeared. Kurtis brought out her sandwich on a heavy ceramic plate, with a paper napkin folded beside it. Riley stared at the plate. She was supposed to eat this on the activity bus to the museum, and a plate was not going to work on her lap while the bus bounced over every pothole on Route 9. "Um," she said. "¿Para el autobús?" Kurtis only shrugged, so she tried pointing at the plate and shaking her head. Kurtis scratched his head with the pencil.

Riley stepped aside to think. Somewhere in the back of her notebook was the vocab list from Monday, and she raced through it in her mind. There had been a phrase about food that left the restaurant, and she could almost see it, something about carrying. She flipped through her notes, and there it was. She marched back to the counter, feeling her heart tick faster, and tried it out, because that was the only way to know if the idea held. "Para llevar," she said.

Kurtis's whole face lit up. "¡Sí, para llevar!" He swept the plate away and returned with the sandwich wrapped in paper, tucked into a bag. Riley wondered whether the phrase literally meant "to take away" or something about carrying, and decided she would look it up later, because the pattern was the interesting part. In Spanish, food to go was not a description of plates or bags; it was a phrase you asked for. She filed that away like a coin in her pocket.

She carried the bag past Caleb, who was already sprinting toward the gym with half a burrito in his hand. Then she stopped, turned around, and went back to Kurtis. "Kurtis, for next time," she said, tapping her notes, "write para llevar on your notepad. Nobody else knows it either." Kurtis grinned and added it in big letters, right under his anonymous alias for the day, "Sr. K."

activity: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
knowledge_domain: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
fact: A symbol is an object, person or event that stands for an idea beyond itself, and a reader must support any meaning they give it with details from the story.
story:
Victoria flipped back to page four for the third time. In Mr. Kapoor's English class they had read "The Lighthouse Keeper," and tomorrow each book club member had to present one symbol from the story and explain what it suggested. She had marked the red door, the storm lantern, and the folded letter, but she couldn't decide which one actually meant something.

Amine leaned across the table. "Easy. The red door means danger. Done."

"It can't just mean danger because you say so," Victoria said. "You have to prove it."

"From the text," Syed added, not looking up from his copy. "That's the whole assignment."

Mr. Kapoor had written one rule on the board, and Victoria had copied it into her notebook word for word: a symbol is an object, person or event that stands for an idea beyond itself, and a reader must support any meaning they give it with details from the story. A diligent student, she had underlined the second half twice. Still, she wanted to test whether the rule held up before she trusted it.

"Try this," she said, sliding the book toward Amine. "Say the red door means danger. Now find three details that support it."

Amine skimmed. "It's red. Red is danger. That's one."

"That's you, not the story. Where does the door show up?"

He ran a finger down the page and stopped. "The keeper paints it right after his brother leaves. And at the end, when the brother comes back, the paint's peeling."

Syed looked up. "So it's not danger. It's the brother. The door stands for him leaving, and it falling apart stands for the family falling apart."

Victoria grabbed her pencil. "Every time the door shows up, the brother gets mentioned. Three for three." She wrote the page numbers beside each one, then sat back. "So the rule works. If we'd just said danger, we'd have nothing to hand in."

The next morning, Amine stood at the front of the class and read their three details aloud. Mr. Kapoor nodded once and marked the rubric. "Supported," he said.

After class he caught Victoria in the hallway. "You figured out how to argue from the text. Want to mentor the newer book club members on it next term? They tend to guess, the way you almost did."

"Almost," Victoria said, and held up her notebook, page numbers still showing.

activity: falling out with a best friend and making up
knowledge_domain: falling out with a best friend and making up
fact: Psychologist Thomas Gordon coined the term 'I-message' in the 1960s: a sentence like 'I felt left out' describes the speaker's feelings instead of blaming the listener with 'you'.
story:
Bodhi hadn't texted Austin back in three days, and Austin was tracking it like a scoreboard. Day one, nothing. Day two, one word: "busy." Day three, nothing again. Austin had sent the venomous message on Wednesday night: "You ditched me at the arcade and told Cassie instead. Nice friend." He'd typed it fast, thumbs hot, and now it just sat there, delivered but never answered.

In his family group chat, Mom posted a photo of lasagna with the caption "DINNER AT 7 CHAMPIONS." His sister sent three thumbs-up. Austin ignored all of it and typed: "does anyone know how to un-send a mean text." His dad replied, "Nope. Fix forward, kiddo."

Fix forward. Great, Dad. Austin flopped on his bed and stared at the ceiling, trying to work out what had actually gone wrong. Bodhi had bailed, sure, but Bodhi had bailed before and it had never turned into radio silence. The difference was the message. Austin read his own words again and noticed a pattern: you, you, you. Every sentence pointed at Bodhi like a finger. Maybe the silence wasn't about the arcade at all. Maybe it was about the pointing.

He typed "how to say sorry without blaming" into the school laptop. A page came up about a psychologist named Thomas Gordon, who coined the term "I-message" back in the 1960s. A sentence like "I felt left out" described the speaker's own feelings instead of blaming the listener with "you." Austin read it twice, then grinned. It was like a secret rule hiding under the whole fight, and nobody had told him. He grabbed his notebook and drafted: "You ditched me." He crossed it out. "I felt left out when you went with Cassie and I heard it from her." His mom appeared in the doorway and said dinner was ready. "In a minute," Austin said. "I'm mediating a crisis." She raised an eyebrow and left him to it.

He tested the idea first. He sent a small I-message to his sister in the family chat: "I felt embarrassed when you showed Mom my bad math quiz." She replied in ten seconds: "ok that's fair, sorry." It worked. Symmetry, almost: the same situation, the same fix. Austin's heart was thumping like he was about to step on stage.

He opened the thread with Bodhi and sent it: "I felt left out when you and Cassie went to the arcade and I found out from her. I miss you. Trampoline park Saturday?" He watched the screen. Delivered. Delivered. Then three dots, and Bodhi's answer burst through: "YES SATURDAY. also I wasn't ignoring you, my phone got confiscated for three days. check the chat."

Austin scrolled up, and there it was, sitting in the family group chat since Wednesday: a message from Bodhi's mom to Austin's mom. "Bodhi lost his phone, poor kid, he's devastated. Tell Austin he says hi."

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
fact: Children and teenagers should not take aspirin during flu or chickenpox, because it is linked to Reye's syndrome, a rare but serious illness affecting the liver and brain.
story:
The headache had moved in behind Audrey's eyes like a bad roommate, and the fever made her bedroom ceiling ripple whenever she blinked. She dragged herself to the bathroom cabinet, where the shelves held cough drops, a thermometer, and one battered bottle of aspirin left over from her mom's bad back. Audrey's hand was halfway to it when she remembered the flu, and a small cold thought slid under her decision: hadn't someone once said aspirin was wrong for kids with flu? She couldn't remember who, or why, and that made her nervous.

She carried the bottle back to her bed and texted Reid, who was at school without her and would be useless until lunch. Then she checked the label herself. Reye's syndrome, the small print said, and she said it out loud, "Reye's syndrome," just to feel the shape of it. She looked it up on her phone: children and teenagers should not take aspirin during flu or chickenpox, because it was linked to Reye's syndrome, a rare but serious illness affecting the liver and brain. Rare. But serious, and it hit the liver and the brain, and Audrey decided that headache or no headache, she would rather not roll those dice. She put the bottle on her nightstand where she could keep an eye on it, as if it might sneak into her on its own.

Her mom came up with soup and found the bottle sitting there like evidence. "You were going to take my aspirin?" she asked, and Audrey shook her head. "I thought about it. Then I read the label. Kids with flu aren't supposed to have aspirin. Something called Reye's syndrome." Her mom sat down on the edge of the bed. "Good. When you had chickenpox in second grade, the doctor made me promise. I was so worried about your fever that night I probably would have given you anything." Audrey remembered that night, suddenly and completely: the itchy spots, the lamp on at two in the morning, her mom reading every bottle before putting each one back. It had looked like doubt. Now it looked like the opposite of doubt, like someone carefully choosing what not to risk.

At lunch, Reid's messages arrived in a pile. He wanted to bring her the history homework, mostly, Audrey suspected, because he'd bombed the last quiz and needed someone to oppose his theory that Mr. Hosseini graded names at random. You're gullible, she typed back. He grades carnivores harder. Ask anyone vegetarian who got an A. Reid replied with a fish emoji and the news that he would come by at four, and also that Jean claimed orange juice cured flu, which Audrey should please not believe.

At four, footsteps clomped up the stairs. Reid appeared in her doorway holding a folder and a grocery bag with three kinds of juice, and behind him Jean's voice called, "Pick the orange one!" Reid held up the bag like a trophy. "We didn't know which you'd want. Jean says you're basically a carnivore anyway, so it doesn't matter."

"Downstairs, both of you," Audrey's mom called from the kitchen, and Reid turned to Jean at the bottom of the steps and said, "Told you we'd get in. Now where's the ice cream."

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Gleaning means gathering crops left in fields after harvest, and some groups send volunteers to glean farms so the produce can go to food banks.
story:
The clipboard said Matteo would be sorting canned goods, but the real problem was in the walk-in cooler, where the vegetable shelf was almost empty. A woman with two kids had just asked if there was anything fresh, and the volunteer at the counter had to shake her head. Matteo stood there holding a bag of dented soup cans, wondering how a food bank in farm country could run out of vegetables.

He found his friends Cedric and Lee stacking boxes of pasta in the back room. "Why is the fridge empty?" Matteo asked. "There are farms everywhere around here."

Lee shrugged. "My uncle works at the farmer's market. He says tons of stuff just gets left in the fields after the machines finish. Potatoes too small for the stores, that kind of thing."

"That can't be right," Cedric said. "Farmers wouldn't just leave food lying around." His tone contradicted his face, though, because he was already pulling out his phone to check.

Before he could type anything, Ms. Ba came in from the loading dock, brushing dirt off her sleeves. She ran the place, and she looked tired but pleased. "Good news," she said. "We've got a generator running in the truck out there, so we can keep things cold. Anyone want to help unload?"

They followed her outside, expecting maybe one crate. There were nine, all heavy with muddy potatoes. "Where did these come from?" Matteo asked.

"A group gleaned them this morning," Ms. Ba said.

"Gleaned?" said Cedric.

"Gleaning means gathering crops left in fields after harvest," she said. "Volunteers go out to farms and pick up what's left over so it can come here." Then she went back inside, because the generator was sputtering and she needed to check the fuel.

Matteo turned the idea over in his head all through the unloading. Farmers couldn't sell the odd-sized potatoes, but that didn't make them any less edible. And if the food bank knew about it, and volunteers knew about it, then the empty shelf wasn't really an empty shelf. It was a full field, twenty minutes away, that nobody had driven to yet.

"Next Saturday," he said, wiping potato mud on his jeans. "We could be the gleaners. All three of us."

Lee held up a potato the exact shape of a duck. "We could call ourselves the Duck Squad."

"We are not calling ourselves the Duck Squad," Cedric said, and put the duck potato carefully on top of the freshest crate.
