activity: to explain how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War
knowledge_domain: to explain how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War
fact: The Treaty of Versailles forbade Germany to unite with Austria, but in March 1938 Hitler annexed Austria, an event called the Anschluss.
story:
Matthew spread the two maps across his grandfather's dining table, weighting the corners with teacups because the old paper refused to lie flat. The first map showed Europe after 1919, the year of the Treaty of Versailles. The second showed Europe in 1939. His history teacher, Mr. Patel, had prescribed a five-minute explanation for Friday: how the treaty helped lead to the Second World War. Matthew had exactly one clue and no idea what to do with it.

"There's a country missing," he said, running a finger down the diagonal border on the earlier map. "Here. Austria. It's just gone on this one."

His grandfather leaned over his shoulder with his glasses pushed up on his forehead, which meant he was pretending he didn't need them. "Gone? Countries don't evaporate, boy. Look again."

Matthew looked again. The second map had Germany stretched bigger, like someone had pulled the eastern edge wider, and there was no Austria at all. He fetched the magnifying glass from the drawer where his grandfather kept it for reading seed packets, and traced the border. Sure enough, the old line between the two countries had vanished, swallowed into one bigger shape. "It's inside Germany," Matthew said. "Somebody glued two countries together. But Mr. Patel said the treaty forbade that. It specifically forbade Germany to unite with Austria."

"So somebody broke the rules," his grandfather said. "What did the teacher call it, this gluing?"

"He didn't call it anything yet. He said we had to find it ourselves." Matthew dug through his backpack and pulled out the library book Mr. Patel had assigned. He flipped past pictures of trenches until he found March 1938. "Here it is. In March 1938 Hitler annexed Austria. And there's a word for it. It's called the Anschluss." He said it twice, slowly, liking the weight of it.

"So the treaty drew a line and said don't cross it," his grandfather said, tapping the map, "and then a man crossed it in front of the whole world, and nobody stopped him." He straightened up and rubbed his back. "Well. That's your explanation, isn't it? A rule is a rule only if someone enforces it."

Matthew sat with that for a moment. Was that how wars started, then, not with a bang but with a broken promise that nobody punished? He turned the idea over the way he turned a puzzle piece, checking which way it fit. The treaty had forbidden the union, and the union had happened anyway, and the bigger Germany on the second map was the proof, sitting right there in ink.

He tried it out loud, speaking to the teacups as if they were Mr. Patel's class. "The Treaty of Versailles forbade Germany to unite with Austria, but in March 1938 Hitler annexed Austria anyway, and that's called the Anschluss." His grandfather applauded with two teacups, clinking them together like cymbals until Matthew rescued them.

"Better than my slideshow about garden slugs," his grandfather said. "Robert fell asleep during the slide about slug mating. Snored into the punch bowl." He shuffled toward the kitchen. "Now explain it once more while I make cocoa, because if you can teach it to a man who thought Austria was a type of cheese, you can teach it to anyone."

Matthew squared the maps, side by side, one country present and one country gone, and began again.

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: In one-point perspective, lines that face you squarely, like window tops and doorframes on a building's front, stay perfectly horizontal or vertical.
story:
Charlie pressed her pencil so hard against the paper that the vanishing point turned into a small gray crater. The assignment was due at the end of art period, and her street drawing was betraying her. The road itself looked fine, shrinking toward the dot in the center of the page, but the bakery and the music shop looked like they had leaned on each other after a long night out.

"You're generating a whole street," Molly said from the next stool, waving her own page, which looked even worse. "Mine looks like an earthquake hit it."

"It's not an earthquake," Charlie said slowly. She held her drawing at arm's length and squinted. Every line she had drawn was tilted, every window frame, every doorway, marching toward the vanishing point like soldiers. That was what Mr. Dela Cruz had shown them on Monday: lines go to the dot. But the real street outside the school did not look like this. The fronts of the buildings, the ones directly across from you, stood flat and square. She thought about the post office she passed every morning, how its big windows ran straight across the brick, level as a pool of water.

"Give me your ruler," she said to Molly. Molly handed it over without argument, which was a mark of true friendship, since Molly guarded her ruler like it was the last one on Earth.

Charlie drew a fresh building. From its front corners she ran two lines back to the vanishing point for the side wall. But the front of the building, the part staring straight at her, she drew with lines that were perfectly horizontal and perfectly vertical. The window tops ran straight across. The doorframe went straight up and down. Then she flattened the paper on the table and looked at it from a low angle, the way you might test ice before stepping on it.

"Oh," Molly said, leaning over. "It's just standing there. Normal. Like a building that has never had a bad day."

"It's the front lines," Charlie said. "The ones facing you. They stay flat. Only the side lines go to the dot." She picked up Molly's ruined earthquake drawing and clipped a fresh sheet to her board for her. "Try the front first. Horizontal across, vertical down."

Mr. Dela Cruz wandered past their table, smelled the turpentine from the paint sink, and sneezed twice. "My allergy to this room is involuntary," he said, dabbing his eyes with a tissue, "unlike the decision to stay and teach it anyway." He looked at Charlie's new building, and one eyebrow went up. He tapped the straight window tops with one finger and kept walking, which in his language was applause.

By the last ten minutes of class, Molly's street had buildings that stood up straight, and Charlie had added a striped awning over her bakery, its front edge running clean and level across the page. She signed her name tiny in the corner, right beside the doorframe she had drawn perfectly, perfectly vertical.

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
knowledge_domain: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
fact: Tropical rainforests lie near the equator, where strong sunlight heats moist air that rises, cools and forms clouds, often bringing heavy afternoon rain.
story:
Anthony spread the two graphs across his grandfather's kitchen table and weighted the corners with salt shakers. One showed a desert, flat lines of heat, barely a whisker of rain all year. The other showed a rainforest, with temperature that barely moved and rainfall bars that climbed like skyscrapers. He had to write a page comparing them for Ms. Chaudhry by Monday, and so far all he had was "the rainforest is wetter," which would earn him the look she gave answers that anyone could say without thinking.

His phone buzzed. Braxton had sent a photo of his own unfinished page, mostly blank, with the message "give me your conclusion when you figure it out." Anthony typed back "no," then set the phone face down, because the graphs bothered him. Every single month, the rainforest bars stayed tall. Rain every month, nearly every day, in a place sitting right on the equator. How did a place get rained on constantly and never dry out? It was like a bathtub that never emptied.

The answer, it turned out, was in the hallway closet. He had gone looking for poster board and found instead a shoebox marked "Amazon, 1989," stuffed with photographs in plastic sleeves. They were authentic, real prints with dates inked on the backs in his grandfather's cramped handwriting, and Anthony went through them one by one. Trees like green towers. A river wide as a highway. And in photo after photo, the same strange pattern: every morning shot showed blue sky, pale and clean, while every afternoon shot showed bruised clouds, rain hammering down, the same river churned to gray. His grandfather had been a foot from the equator, and it had stormed on him every single afternoon.

Anthony grabbed paper and made two columns, morning and afternoon, and counted the photos like data points. The morning skies were clear in every one. The afternoon storms came in every one. Then he thought about the sunlight, which at the equator beats down hard all year, and the moist air rising off all that jungle, cooling into those towering clouds. He remembered Braxton once dismantling an old radio to see what was inside; this was the same thing, except what he was taking apart was a pattern hiding inside thirty-year-old photographs.

"Grandpa," he called toward the living room, "did it rain every afternoon when you were there?"

"Like clockwork," his grandfather called back. "Blue skies at breakfast, storms by four."

Anthony wrote his conclusion, then texted Braxton one line: the rainforest gets its rain the same way every day, near the equator, strong sunlight heats the moist air, it rises, cools, forms clouds, and the afternoon pours down. Then he cleared the salt shakers and put the photographs back in their sleeves, keeping out the one of the storm over the river, flat and gleaming under the kitchen light.

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: A percentage based on very few attempts can be misleading: a player who makes one shot out of one attempt shoots 100 percent.
story:
Charles had taped a chart to the gym door ranking every player on the school basketball team by shooting percentage, and he updated it after each practice with a pencil stub he kept in his sock. Before Wednesday's practice, a crowd had formed around the chart, and Levi was standing in front of it with his arms crossed, grinning.

"Number one," Levi said. "One hundred percent. Read it and weep, Rudy."

Rudy leaned in and squinted. "You've made one shot all season. One shot out of one attempt. That's it."

"A hundred percent is a hundred percent," Levi said. "The chart doesn't lie."

Charles felt his stomach tighten. He had built the chart to rank the best shooters, and now it was crowning a player who had taken a single shot all season while Rudy, who had taken forty, sat lower down. He tried to figure out the problem, turning it over on the walk to class. The chart wasn't lying exactly, but it wasn't telling the whole truth either. It treated one shot and forty shots the same way, and he could see how that made the whole list biased toward people who barely played. After school he found Ms. Nowak in the hallway and asked if he could borrow the gym for ten minutes.

"You'll have to sweep when you're done," she said. "And don't retire that chart of yours. The team loves it."

"I'm not retiring it," Charles said. "I'm testing it."

At practice, he pulled Levi and Rudy aside. "One round each," Charles said. "Ten free throws, same as always. If the chart's fair, Levi should stay perfect."

Levi shrugged and stepped to the line. His first shot clanged off the rim. His second one banked in. He made two out of ten, and Charles wrote it down while Levi watched his percentage sink like a stone in a bucket.

"Seventy-five percent now," Charles said, doing the math against his old numbers. "Three out of four."

"Because I actually shot the ball," Levi said slowly. He stared at the paper. "Okay. I get it. One shot out of one attempt, and I was walking around calling myself perfect." He looked at Rudy. "You've taken like forty. That's the real number one."

"That's his motive, by the way," Rudy said, jabbing a thumb at Charles. "He's not doing this to embarrass you."

Levi picked up the ball and bounced it twice. "Ten more," he said. "Count them this time. All of them."

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: Psychologist Lee Ross named the fundamental attribution error in 1977: the tendency to blame others' actions on their personality while underestimating their situation.
story:
Ryder pushed his noodles around the plate and said, "Oakley slammed the door in my face today. In front of everyone. He's turning into a jerk." The kitchen smelled of garlic, and his fork clicked against the bowl with every stab.

"Whole story?" his dad asked, passing the bread.

"He walked into class late, ignored my wave, and when I followed him into the hallway he shoved past me and shut the door." Ryder took a bite, chewing hard. "Mr. Wright tried to diagnose the problem, asking Oakley questions, but Oakley just stared at the desk like the room was arid, no water anywhere. He never does that. He's the one who laughs loudest at lunch."

His little sister knocked her cup over, and while his dad mopped it up, Ryder remembered something. At the start of the year, Mr. Wright had written a phrase on the board during a unit on how people think. Ryder pulled out his phone under the table and found his photo of that board. "Fundamental attribution error," he read aloud. Below it, in his own handwriting from that day, he had copied the whole sentence: psychologist Lee Ross named the fundamental attribution error in 1977, the tendency to blame others' actions on their personality while underestimating their situation. He read it twice, and a cold, tickly feeling crawled up his neck. He had decided Oakley was a jerk. He had not once wondered what Oakley's day had been like.

"Can I be excused for five minutes?" he asked. His dad nodded, so Ryder grabbed the notebook he kept in his backpack and wrote a note, then folded it into a paper airplane, the way he and Oakley had done in fourth grade. His plan was simple: instead of accusing, he would ask what happened. If Oakley answered, Ryder would know whether the problem was Oakley's personality or Oakley's situation.

At school the next morning, he sailed the plane onto Oakley's desk before the bell. At dinner that night, Ryder could hardly sit still, because Oakley's reply was folded in his pocket. He smoothed it out next to the mashed potatoes. "My dog died Tuesday morning," it read. "I was late because I couldn't stop crying, and I shoved the door because if you said one kind word I was going to lose it in front of everybody. Sorry. You're the only one who asked." The paper had a small tear in the corner and a smudge, like someone had pressed a thumb there for a long time.

Ryder read it out loud to his dad. "I almost decided he was a mean person," he said, "when really he was just having the worst day of his life." His dad squeezed his shoulder. Ryder picked up his pen and, on the bottom of Oakley's note, wrote back: "Want to come over Saturday? We can build something."

activity: to change a flat bicycle tyre using tyre levers and a pump
knowledge_domain: to change a flat bicycle tyre using tyre levers and a pump
fact: A slow leak can be found by pumping some air into the tube and holding it under water to watch for bubbles.
story:
Noah knelt on the concrete behind the gym, where Ms. Watanabe had set out a bucket of soapy water, a floor pump, and three tyre levers shaped like fat plastic spoons. The bike in front of him had a rear tyre gone soft as an old orange, and the deal was simple: get it rolling by the end of lunch, and he could ride home with Payton and Omer instead of taking the bus with the trumpet case.

He wedged the first lever under the bead of the tyre, then the second, and worked the rim free the way Ms. Watanabe had shown the whole class. When he pulled out the tube, he squeezed it and listened. Nothing. No hiss anywhere along its length. He remembered his grandfather's garage last summer, the two of them crouched over a tub of water with a tube from an old lawn mower, watching a thin string of bubbles rise from a pinhole so small you could never find it by looking. His grandfather had pumped some air in first, then dipped the tube a section at a time, and the bubbles had marked the spot like a flag.

"We checked the whole thing," Omer said, watching him roll the tube loosely in his hands. "You're going to sit here all lunch."

Noah didn't answer. He attached the pump, gave the tube maybe thirty strokes until it was firm, and lowered one end into the bucket. Nothing. He moved it along, hand over hand, rotating it under the surface. Halfway through, a tiny stream of bubbles came up from the side of the tube, steady as a whisper, from a spot with no visible hole at all. "There it is," he said, and held his thumb on the wet patch so he wouldn't lose it.

"You inferred that from silence?" Payton said. "Squeezing it and hearing nothing?"

"I inferred it from my grandfather's tub," Noah said. "The bubbles tell you where. You can't see it any other way."

Ms. Watanabe handed him a patch kit. He roughed the spot with the sandpaper, spread the glue, waited until it went dull, and pressed the patch on hard while Omer counted to sixty out loud, too fast, then again, slower. Noah worked the tube back inside the tyre, pushed the bead over the rim with his thumbs the last stretch, and connected the pump. The gauge climbed to forty and held. He spun the wheel and watched it turn clean and true.

"Race you to the gate," Omer said, already swinging onto his own bike.

Noah shoved off after him, and the patched tyre hummed against the pavement all the way past the goalposts.

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: Typing a message in all capital letters is widely read as shouting in online communication.
story:
Madison sat at the kitchen computer with her math homework open in one window and the group chat in the other. The chat was for planning the science fair project, but lately it had gone quiet, and nobody had answered her last three messages about the poster board. She needed it bought by Saturday, and it was already Thursday.

Then the chat lit up. Kianna had typed, all in capital letters, "WHERE IS EVERYBODY." A moment later Cristiano replied, "why are you yelling?" Kianna sent a single question mark. Madison leaned closer to the screen. She scrolled up through the chat and noticed something: the messages in all caps got answered fast, every time, while the lowercase ones sat there for hours. Even her own polite "does anyone know about the poster board" had vanished into silence.

She turned her chair sideways and chewed the end of her pen. Maybe people just noticed the big letters more. Or maybe they read them as shouting and rushed to respond, the way you'd turn around if someone yelled your name in a hallway. She couldn't see the rule itself, but she could test it. She typed, in caps, "I NEED AN ANSWER ABOUT THE POSTER BOARD BY TONIGHT." Her finger hovered over the enter key. It felt rude, like shoving through a door. At home, in a private chat with one friend, she would never write that way. But this was a public room with six people in it, and apparently the loud kid got heard.

She pressed enter. Cristiano answered within a minute: "my dad can get poster board tomorrow." Kianna wrote, "you don't have to shout," and added a laughing face, so it wasn't a real scolding. Madison typed back in lowercase, "sorry, testing something." Then, quieter: "I cherish this group, I promise."

Cristiano sent, "you're so gullible, Kianna replied to you in nine seconds."

"Nine seconds is a privilege," Kianna answered. "Earn it."

Madison smiled, closed the chat window, and wrote Saturday's date at the top of her homework page.

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: Hypotheses are often written as 'If ..., then ...' statements, which name the change being made and the result that is predicted.
story:
Maya counted the strawberries on the kitchen windowsill and came up one short. She had counted nine after school, and now there were eight, and nobody in her house would admit to touching them.

"I didn't eat it," her brother said, without looking up from his game.

"I didn't say you did." But she had, sort of. Somebody had a motive, and the list of suspects was short: him, her mother, or something she couldn't see. She set the container back on the sill and noticed a tiny red smear on the tiles below. Too low for her brother, unless he had crouched there eating strawberries like a raccoon.

She called Jayde from the couch, phone wedged against her shoulder. "If I set out one strawberry on the floor at night, then it'll be gone by morning if something is coming in low," she said.

"That's a real hypothesis," Jayde said. "Ms. Wang made us write them like that last week. If something, then something. You have to name what you're changing and what you predict will happen."

"Then my hypothesis is that a mouse is stealing my strawberries." Maya got a pencil and wrote it on the back of a receipt so it would sound official.

She had planned to stake out the kitchen at midnight, but her mother postponed that idea fast. "You have school. Set a camera if you're so curious." They didn't have a camera, so Maya rigged a temporary alarm instead: a baking sheet balanced on the counter edge, with one strawberry in the middle of it as bait. If anything bumped the sheet, it would clang onto the floor and wake the whole apartment.

At two in the morning, the clang woke the whole apartment. Maya ran in with her phone flashlight and caught a flash of gray tail vanishing behind the refrigerator, where she now saw a gap in the baseboard about the width of her fist.

"Ha!" she said to the empty kitchen. The hypothesis had held up. She felt a little smug until the morning, when Aubrie, sitting on her front steps before the bus came, poked a hole in it.

"Maybe it's not a mouse. Could be a rat. Or a squirrel." Aubrie bit her bagel. "Your test just proves something took the bait."

"Fine. New hypothesis." Maya thought it through. "If I put flour in front of the hole, then I'll get footprints, and footprints will tell me what it is." She wrote that one down too, on a fresh receipt, and taped the flour tray to the floor before school so nobody could call it an accident.

The next morning there were tracks. Tiny ones, four toes, dragging tail line through the white dust. She photographed them and slid the print under Ms. Wang's door with a note: "Hypothesis confirmed. Can you tell me what this is?"

The note came back within the hour, one word circled twice in red ink: mouse.

Maya stood in the hallway holding the paper. "All right," she said. "Then here's my next one. If I plug that hole, then you're somebody else's problem."

activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
knowledge_domain: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
fact: Blocking is rejecting or ignoring a partner's offer, such as saying 'we're not on a boat', and it usually stops the scene from moving forward.
story:
The stage lights at the community theatre were half-blown, so the rehearsal space felt like an old photograph, warm in some corners and shadowed in others. Alexia stood in a circle with six other kids while Mr. Oliveira shuffled index cards he never seemed to read. "Partner scenes," he said. "Alexia and Finnley, you're up. Whatever your partner gives you, take it somewhere."

Finnley grinned and launched in immediately. "Wow, this boat is really rocking." She planted her feet wide and gripped an imaginary rail.

"We're not on a boat," Alexia said. "We're in the cafeteria."

The laughter from the other kids cut off like a faucet turning. Finnley's arms dropped to her sides and she blinked, unsure where to go next. Someone in the circle whispered something Alexia couldn't hear, and then everyone just stood there while the scene sagged into silence. Mr. Oliveira made a small note on his card, which somehow felt louder than any critique.

She sat out the next round and watched Cristian go up with a boy she didn't know. Cristian opened with "Hand me that wrench, the rocket's about to launch," and the other boy, without hesitating, grabbed an invisible wrench and said, "Careful, it's the one that fell in the soup." The scene propelled forward from there, ending with the two of them slurping rocket fuel out of bowls while the circle cracked up. Alexia found herself wondering what had actually just happened, because Cristian's partner had said something completely random, and instead of fixing it, Cristian had poured it into the story. She thought back to her own scene. Finnley had offered a boat, and Alexia had said no. Was that the whole problem, a scene dying from one little word?

She tapped Finnley's shoulder. "Can we go again?"

"We're not on a boat," Finnley said, half teasing, half not.

"Okay, but next time it comes up, watch me," Alexia said. When Mr. Oliveira called for a second round, she walked to center stage with Finnley and waited. Finnley started the same way, hands on the rail, the boat rocking. Alexia grabbed the rail beside her. "I told you the settlement on this island was a bad idea," she said. "The natives asked for our anchor as rent."

Finnley's whole face changed, and she leaned into the wind. "Then we row, and we argue about it later." The circle was laughing again, and this time Alexia was laughing too, the scene pulling her forward like a current she'd finally stopped swimming against.

Afterward Mr. Oliveira caught her by the door. "You figured it out, didn't you?"

Alexia nodded. "Blocking," she said. "It kills the scene."

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Details in the background of a photo, such as a street sign, a house number or a school logo, can let a stranger work out where it was taken.
story:
Lydia leaned against the railing outside the smoothie shop at the mall, holding her phone at arm's length while Katrina and Carina squeezed into the frame. "One more," Carina said, "Ms. Zhu said she wants a picture from our science fair celebration." Behind them, the food court sign showed the mall's name and, farther back, the glass doors with the street visible through them.

"Wait," Lydia said. She pulled the phone in and zoomed in on the shot she had just taken. Behind Katrina's shoulder, through the doors, she could read a street sign. She zoomed further. A house number was visible above the doorway of the shop across the road, and beyond that, the corner of Carina's apartment building, the one with the blue awning.

"What's wrong?" Katrina asked, peeling the wrapper off her straw.

"I can see your street sign in this," Lydia said. "And your building, Carina. Anyone looking at this could figure out exactly where we are." She scrolled back through the last few photos. The one from the arcade had the mall directory in the corner. The one from the bench showed the store directory with the cross streets printed on it.

"So?" Carina said. "It's just Ms. Zhu."

"It is, if she's the only one who ever sees it," Lydia said. "But what if she forwards it? What if someone else posts it?" She tried an experiment. She zoomed in on the arcade photo until the directory filled the screen, then searched the cross streets on a map. In ten seconds she was looking at a satellite view of the mall, and the parking lot where her mom had dropped them off.

Katrina set down her smoothie. "Okay, that's creepy."

"It's not magic," Lydia said. "It's just the background. A street sign, a house number, a school logo. Any of those can let a stranger work out where a photo was taken."

Carina looked at the glass doors with her lips pressed together, then at the warm smoothie in her hand. "Could we take it somewhere with a neutral background? Like that plain wall by the bookstore?"

Lydia checked the wall. Nothing on it but beige paint. She framed the three of them against it, made sure the doors were behind her own back, and took the shot. "Send Ms. Zhu this one," she said. "And Carina, I'll cite you as the one who found the wall, since you're the reason it works."

Carina grinned and held up her smoothie like a trophy. Katrina wiped a drip off Lydia's phone case without being asked and said, "Lens is clean now, too. Say cheese."

activity: to explain how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War
knowledge_domain: to explain how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War
fact: The Treaty of Versailles, which ended the First World War between Germany and the Allies, was signed on 28 June 1919 in the Hall of Mirrors at the Palace of Versailles.
story:
Blake slid the photograph across the table until it sat under the lamp. Men in stiff suits, crowded around a long table, and behind them, mirrors, dozens of them, climbing the walls. He had four hours before his presentation, and his poster board was blank except for one question in marker: How did a treaty start another war?

"You're supposed to be finding sources," Enzo said, stacking the archive boxes Ms. Swampy had pulled for them. "Not staring at pictures."

"This is a source." Blake tapped the glass. "Look at the room. Who signs a treaty in a hall made of mirrors?"

Sage leaned over his shoulder. "Vain people," she said. "Men who wanted to watch themselves win."

Blake pulled the folder's index card closer. He read it twice, then a third time. "It says here the Treaty of Versailles was signed on 28 June 1919 in the Hall of Mirrors at the Palace of Versailles. That's the treaty that ended the First World War, between Germany and the Allies." He wrote it down, word for word, the way Ms. Swampy insisted. Dates could betray you if you trusted memory.

"Okay, so it ended a war," Enzo said. "Your poster asks how it started one. Different question."

Blake laid out index cards in a row, one per event, like dominoes. He had learned the trick from his sister, who studied chemistry: you can't see a hidden cause, but you can test whether one thing pushes the next. First card: the treaty. Last card: the Second World War. Between them, a gap of blank cards. "If the treaty helped cause the war, something has to go in the middle. Something the treaty did to Germany."

Sage was already flipping through a newspaper from the 1930s, the pages brittle and yellow, ink saturating the paper so deeply that some columns had bled through to the back. "Here," she said. "Complaints about the treaty. Every year, the same complaints, louder every year." She set the paper on the table. "Some politician calls it venomous. A poison, they mean."

Blake turned the card over and wrote anger, then crossed it out and wrote anger that grew. He placed it in the gap and pressed the first domino down with his finger. "The treaty ends one war," he said quietly. "The anger from it feeds the next one." He looked up. "The mirrors, though. Germany signed it in France's palace, in a hall built to glorify a whole dynasty. Imagine signing your defeat in a room like that."

Enzo picked up the marker and wrote the date on the poster in big letters. "28 June 1919. Hall of Mirrors. Now the board's not blank."

Blake set the photograph at the center and taped down the corners.

activity: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs
knowledge_domain: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs
fact: French speakers ask a price with "C'est combien ?" or "Combien ça coûte ?", both meaning "How much is it?"
story:
Lily sat in the back row of Mr. Ito's French class, wishing the ceiling fan would spin faster. It whirred above them like a small turbine, pushing the warm air around without actually cooling anything. On the board, Mr. Ito had written two phrases, and Lily copied them into her notebook for the third time, hoping the letters would finally stick in her head.

"Practise ordering," Mr. Ito said, clapping his hands. "Partners. Alyvia, you're the waiter. Audrina, you're hungry."

Audrina rubbed her stomach and announced, "Je voudrais un croissant," with such drama that half the class laughed. When it was Lily's turn, she froze. Last week she had skipped practising with the class crêpe menu because she'd figured she already knew enough words, and now that choice felt like a mistake she couldn't undo. Tomorrow the French club was walking to the real crêpe stand on Miller Street, and she had exactly four euros in her pocket, which might be enough or might not.

At lunch, Lily spread her notes on the table. "Alyvia, if I only remember one thing tomorrow, which thing should it be?"

"How to ask the price," Alyvia said immediately. She pointed at Lily's notebook. "You say 'C'est combien?' or 'Combien ça coûte?' They both mean 'How much is it?' Two ways, same question."

Lily stared at the two phrases. She liked that there were two doors into the same room. If she panicked and blurted the wrong one, it would still work, which seemed almost too generous for a language that had forty ways to spell one sound.

The next afternoon, the class lined up at the crêpe stand while Mr. Ito pretended not to supervise. The smell of butter made Lily's stomach announce itself loudly, and Audrina whispered, "Imminent collapse," which made Lily laugh so hard she almost lost her place in line. When her turn came, the man behind the griddle raised his eyebrows at her.

"Bonjour," Lily said, her voice steadier than she expected. "Je voudrais une crêpe au chocolat." He nodded and flipped the batter. While it browned, she counted her four euros in her pocket and realized she had never checked whether chocolate cost more. She took a breath.

"Combien ça coûte?" she asked.

"Trois euros cinquante," he said.

Fifty cents to spare. Lily handed over the coins, took the warm paper cone, and turned to find Alyvia grinning at her.

"Told you," Alyvia said.

"You told me," Lily said, and took an enormous bite.

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: Bones grow longer at growth plates near their ends, and once these plates close after puberty, a person stops getting taller.
story:
Alice had measured herself against the locker room door frame that morning, and the pencil mark was barely a finger's width above the one from September. In September she had shot up almost an inch in six weeks. Now, it seemed, she had stopped.

Joelle was already changed and sitting on the bench, lacing her shoes. "You're staring at that mark again."

"Half an inch since fall," Alice said. "Maybe less."

"Mr. Fortin says girls finish growing before boys do. It's not fair, but it's true." Joelle stood and bounced a basketball twice. "Dominik grew two inches over winter break. He rubs it in every practice."

Dominik chose that moment to come around the corner, gym bag over his shoulder and a folded paper in his hand. "Alice. Joelle. Look at this." He unfolded it on the bench. It was a printout of an X-ray, grey and ghostly, a wrist and hand with the bones showing dark and thin. "I broke my wrist at my cousin's place last month. The doctor gave me the films."

"You brought your own bones to the locker room," Joelle said.

"The doctor said these dark lines near the ends, see, they're growth plates. Bones grow longer at the growth plates near their ends." Dominik tapped the gaps at the ends of the finger bones. "He said once the plates close after puberty, you stop getting taller. Mine are still open, so I keep going."

Alice leaned in. The dark lines were plain once you knew where to look, running like seams across the ends of the bones. She thought about her own hands, her own September growth spurt, her slow mother and her tall father. There was no way to see her own plates, but the doctor's rule worked both ways, didn't it? If open plates meant still growing, then a spurt that stopped could mean the plates were closing.

"How do you know if yours are closed?" she asked.

"You'd need an X-ray," Dominik said. "Nobody X-rays you for fun."

Alice picked up the printout and held it to the light. "Then you can't know. Not from a pencil mark on a door." She set it down carefully, as if the paper might break too. "One more measurement won't tell me anything. Being diligent about it doesn't help if the thing you're measuring can't be seen."

The coach's whistle shrilled through the door. Joelle grabbed the ball and Dominik stuffed the X-ray into his bag, and the three of them ran out onto the court, where the ceiling was high and the marks on the wall meant nothing at all.
